objective: Evaluating aspects of a Sustainability Management Plan against a scenario: anti-bribery standards and supporting community/social-responsibility development
secondaryObjectives: Identifying the project manager's role and responsibilities in implementing a Sustainability Management Plan, including systems-thinking concepts and distinguishing PM/sponsor/PMO roles

sources.cite: PMI, Certified Sustainable Project Professional (CSPP) bundle and exam page: P5 Standard: Sustainability and Impact Analysis 24% (the largest domain with PRiSM Life Cycle Approach 23% and Project Management Considerations 23%)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 directly (summarizing fetch of pmi.org/certifications/cspp-bundle-exam-course). The page lists six domains: Foundations of Sustainable Project Work 12%, PRiSM Life Cycle Approach 23%, P5 Standard: Sustainability and Impact Analysis 24%, Developing a Sustainability Management Plan 12%, ESG & Sustainability Reporting, Governance, and Project Communications 7%, Project Management Considerations 23% (they add to 101%). It says the P5 Standard evaluates project impacts on 'people, planet, and prosperity', and a prep module practices 'a P5 Impact Analysis' to 'identify, assess and mitigate sustainability impacts'. The course seed's five domains and weights (P5 36%) differ from this page; the P5 domain is the largest either way. The objective wording is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's cspp-school-laptop-p5-review (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You manage a highway upgrade abroad for a fictional engineering firm. A local permitting agent offers to 'speed up' permits for a fee.
handover: The sustainability management plan covers emissions and waste, but not ethics or community.
Villages along the route lose farmland to the road.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: the payment surfaces in an audit; the firm self-reports and is barred from bidding for public contracts for a year.
Week 3: farmers block the site for a week over compensation; the schedule slips.
Week 4: grievances pile up unanswered for two months; nobody owns them.

abcPrompt.title: A fee to speed up permits
abcPrompt.context: The fee is outside any official schedule.

choices.label: Refuse, report it to compliance, and add anti-bribery controls to the plan (due diligence on agents, a gifts register, reporting channel)

effects.log: The payment is refused; controls are added.

choices.feedback: Anti-bribery standards forbid facilitation payments; the plan needs controls.

choices.label: Ask the client if it's normal locally
choices.feedback: It delays the refusal and suggests it might be acceptable.

choices.label: Pay the fee as a local cost of business
choices.feedback: It's a bribe under the firm's code and international law.

communityPrompt.title: Farmers losing land
communityPrompt.context: No hiring plan or grievance channel exists.

choices.label: Add local hiring and training targets, fair compensation, a grievance channel and a community investment fund, agreed with village representatives
choices.feedback: Social responsibility belongs in the plan, agreed with the people affected.

choices.label: Donate to a local school
choices.feedback: Kind, but not a plan with the affected people.

choices.label: Leave compensation to the government
choices.feedback: The affected farmers have no voice in the project.

choices.label: Add leading indicators (training hours, grievances resolved within 30 days, agent due-diligence completed) to the lagging ones, reviewed monthly by you
choices.feedback: Leading indicators show trouble early; the project manager owns implementation.

choices.label: Keep the end-of-project measures
choices.feedback: Problems show only when it's too late.

choices.label: Hand the plan to the environmental officer
choices.feedback: Implementation is the project manager's responsibility across the project.

reflection.question: Write the updated sustainability management plan summary.

parts.label: Ethics and community
parts.criteria: Payment refused; due diligence, gifts register and reporting; hiring, compensation, grievance and fund.
parts.modelAnswer: We refused the permit fee and added anti-bribery controls; the villages agreed hiring, compensation, a grievance channel and a fund.

parts.label: Monitoring
parts.criteria: Leading and lagging indicators reviewed monthly by the project manager.
parts.modelAnswer: Training hours, grievance resolution and agent checks lead; waste and emissions lag; I review them monthly.

scoring.modelReasoning: A sustainability management plan covers ethics and social responsibility as well as environment: anti-bribery controls and refusal of facilitation payments, community development agreed with the people affected, and leading as well as lagging indicators. The project manager owns its implementation.
